theory.text: The AI was trained on a snapshot of the world. That snapshot has a date — the knowledge cutoff. Anything that changed after it doesn't exist as far as the model knows: new framework versions, new APIs, deprecated methods, fresh syntax.

When you don't pin a version, the AI averages across years. You get code that looks plausible but uses Next.js 13 patterns in a Next.js 15 project, or a library API that was renamed last quarter. The build breaks, you waste an hour, you blame the AI. The real fix is upstream: tell it the version.

theory.label: Pin the version, save the hour
theory.text:
❌ 'Add a server action.'
✅ 'Add a Next.js 15 server action using async/await syntax. App Router. The form should call it directly via the action prop.'
If something the AI suggests doesn't exist or doesn't work, suspect the version before you suspect yourself. Then re-prompt with the exact version pinned.

exercise.prompt_template: Always pin the [BLANK] of your stack, because the AI has a knowledge [BLANK] and may not know recent changes.

blanks.hint_1: Next.js 13? Next.js 15? Which one are you on?
blanks.hint_2: It's the number after the framework name — '15', '4.6', etc.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'version' (or 'release'). Naming the version cuts the AI's guessing space dramatically.

blanks.hint_1: What ends the AI's awareness of the world?
blanks.hint_2: It's the date after which nothing in the model's training exists.
blanks.explanation: The answer is 'cutoff' (or 'date'). After the cutoff, the AI is genuinely guessing — and confidently.

outro.recap: You learned to pin versions and to suspect the cutoff when something looks plausible but breaks.
outro.next_prompt: Last lesson: build your own personal library of prompts you can reuse.
